prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We’re all dreamers; we don’t know who we are. Some machine made us; machine of the world, the constricting family. Then back to the world, polished by soft whips. We dream; we don’t remember. Machine of the family: dark fur, forests of the mother’s body. Machine of the mother: white city inside her. And before that: earth and water. Moss between rocks, pieces of leaves and grass. And before, cells in a great darkness. And before that, the veiled world. This is why you were born: to silence me. Cells of my mother and father, it is your turn to be pivotal, to be the masterpiece. I improvised; I never remembered. Now it’s your turn to be driven; you’re the one who demands to know: Why do I suffer? Why am I ignorant? Cells in a great darkness. Some machine made us; it is your turn to address it, to go back asking what am I for? What am I for?

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- We are dreamers shaped by forces we do not fully understand, including the world and the family.
- Human existence is traced backward through the mother, nature, cells, and an unknowable, veiled origin.
- Each generation inherits the task of becoming pivotal and creating meaning from what came before.
- Suffering and ignorance drive the search for self-knowledge and purpose.
- The central question of existence is, “What am I for?”
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text explores identity, origins, suffering, and purpose through a recursive, dreamlike journey backward from family and motherhood to nature, cells, and a veiled primordial world. It suggests that each generation inherits the task of confronting its creation and ignorance, making the search for meaning—“What am I for?”—a pivotal human responsibility.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Some, Then, Machine

outputs.L1:
We are all dreamers; we do not know who we are. Some machine made us—the machine of the world, the constricting family—and then sent us back into the world, polished by soft whips. We dream; we do not remember.

The machine of the family: dark fur, forests of the mother’s body. The machine of the mother: a white city within her. And before that: earth and water, moss between rocks, fragments of leaves and grass. And before that, cells in a great darkness. And before that, the veiled world.

This is why you were born: to silence me. Cells of my mother and father, it is your turn to become pivotal, to become the masterpiece. I improvised; I never remembered. Now it is your turn to be driven. You are the one who demands to know: Why do I suffer? Why am I ignorant?

Cells in a great darkness. Some machine made us; it is your turn to confront it, to return and ask: What am I for? What am I for?
outputs.L2:
Every one of us lives in dreams, uncertain of our true identity. We were produced by a mechanism—the machinery of existence, the confining structure of family—and then returned to the wider world, refined by gentle lashes. We sleep inside our visions and retain no memory.

The family is a mechanism of shadowy fur and forests formed from the mother’s flesh. The mother, too, is a mechanism, holding a pale city within her. Earlier came soil and water: moss wedged among stones, fragments of foliage, blades of grass. Earlier still, there were cells suspended in immense darkness; before even that lay a hidden world.

You came into being for this reason: to make me quiet. Cells inherited from my mother and father, the decisive role now belongs to you; you must become the masterwork. I made things up as I went and recalled nothing. Now you must be propelled forward. You are the one insisting on answers: Why is there pain in me? Why do I lack understanding?

Cells remain in the vast dark. A mechanism created us, and now you must confront it. You must retrace the path and keep demanding: What purpose do I serve? What purpose do I serve?
outputs.L3:
We are dreamers, shaped by forces we can sense but never fully understand. The world enters us through history, culture, circumstance, and chance, while the family gives us our first language of love, fear, belonging, and identity. Long before we begin to choose who we will become, these forces have already left their marks upon us.

If we trace human existence backward, we return first to the mother, then to nature, to the living cell, and finally to an origin hidden behind the veil of time. We can study the processes that brought us here, but the ultimate source remains unknowable. Our beginnings are both intimate and mysterious: we come from particular bodies and families, yet also from a vast continuity of life whose deepest cause escapes us.

Every generation inherits this unfinished story. It receives the consequences, memories, wounds, and achievements of those who came before, but it is not required merely to repeat them. Its task is to become pivotal—to transform inheritance into possibility and to create meaning from what has been given. In doing so, each generation becomes a bridge between the past and a future it cannot fully foresee.

The search for meaning often begins in suffering and ignorance. Pain exposes the limits of our understanding, while uncertainty compels us to ask who we are and why we are here. These questions may not yield final answers, but they drive us toward self-knowledge, responsibility, and purpose.

At the heart of existence, then, lies a question deeper than “What am I?” or “Where did I come from?” It is the question that turns identity into direction and life into vocation: **What am I for?**
outputs.L4:
I begin with my mother, because that is where every story of the self seems to begin. Before I had a name, before I knew the difference between my body and the world, I lived within her. Her blood carried what I needed; her movements shaped my first sense of time. Yet she, too, began inside another body. Behind her stood her mother, and behind that mother another, each life nested within a life that came before it.

If I follow this line backward, the familiar faces gradually disappear. Names are lost first, then photographs, houses, languages, and histories. The mothers become shadows. Their particular griefs are forgotten, though their consequences remain. Their fears survive as warnings, their hungers as habits, their wounds as silences passed from parent to child.

Perhaps inheritance is not merely the transmission of blood. Perhaps we also inherit unfinished questions.

My mother asked who she was, even if she never spoke the words aloud. Her mother must have asked in her own way. Each generation awakens inside a world it did not make, carrying a body it did not choose, surrounded by explanations offered by people who are themselves uncertain. We are told where we came from, what we should love, what we should fear, and what kind of life counts as good. Eventually, if we are fortunate—or if suffering leaves us no alternative—we begin to question what we have been given.

Why was I made this way? Why was I made at all?

In the dream, I continue moving backward. The human figures dissolve into animals: warm bodies breathing in darkness, creatures searching for food, shelter, and one another. Their eyes contain no histories that I can read, yet they know pain. They protect their young. They flee danger. They call out when separated. The distance between their lives and mine begins to narrow.

Farther back, fur gives way to scales, scales to soft tissue, limbs to fins. The world becomes water. Identity no longer belongs to a face or a name but to a pattern struggling to continue. A body divides. A cell encloses itself against the surrounding dark. Something without language distinguishes between inside and outside, nourishment and poison, survival and dissolution.

Was this the first self?

I go back again, beyond memory, beyond motherhood as I understand it. There are no hands to hold an infant, no mouths to speak a name. There are only molecules meeting, separating, and meeting again. Chance repeats itself until repetition begins to resemble intention. Matter organizes. Boundaries form. The first fragile structures persist long enough to copy themselves, though imperfectly. From those imperfections come variation, adaptation, and eventually every living thing that will suffer beneath the sun.

The journey should end there, but it does not. Behind the earliest cell stands another darkness: a veiled world of heat, stone, water, and violent skies. Behind that world are stars forging the elements from which oceans, bones, blood, and thought will be made. Behind the stars is a beginning I cannot see. Every answer opens into a deeper ignorance.

The veil never lifts completely.

I return to myself with no final explanation. I am still the child of my mother, and she is still the child of hers. I am also the descendant of animals without names, of cells without minds, of matter shaped in ancient stars. All these origins exist within me, yet none of them alone can tell me what my life means.

To know how something came into being is not the same as knowing what it is for.

That is the burden each generation inherits. We are created by forces we do not understand—by parents, histories, bodies, accidents, and desires—and then asked to confront that creation. We must decide what to accept, what to forgive, what to resist, and what must not be passed onward. We must look directly at the ignorance of those who made us without forgetting that our own children, and the future itself, may one day judge our ignorance in turn.

Suffering makes this responsibility unavoidable. Pain asks whether existence is merely something to endure. Loss asks what can remain when everything we love is temporary. The past asks whether repetition is destiny. No inherited answer is sufficient, because each life must encounter these questions in its own body.

“What am I for?”

The question is not a demand for a predetermined function, as though a human being were a tool designed for a single use. It is an invitation—and a warning. If purpose is not simply given to us by our origins, then we must participate in making it. We must transform inheritance into choice, suffering into understanding, and ignorance into attention.

Perhaps this is what it means to become human: not to escape the vast chain of creation, but to become conscious of it. To recognize the mothers behind us, the creatures within us, the cells beneath us, and the hidden world beyond our knowledge—and still to answer for the life we shape.

We do not choose the mystery from which we emerge. But we are responsible for what we bring out of it.
outputs.L5:
Some said the old machine had been silent for decades. Then, one stormy night, its gears began to turn. Lights flickered across its metal frame, and a message appeared:

“Some dreams only wait for the right moment to awaken.”

Then the machine opened its door, revealing not wires or engines, but a garden filled with stars.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about birth, ancestry, family, and existential suffering, using recurring imagery of machines, cells, darkness, forests, and the mother’s body. End by repeating the question “What am I for?”
counterfactuals.output:
I was born in the engine room of my mother,  
where red pistons lifted the dark  
and every cell carried a locked forest.

Behind me stood the ancestral machines—  
grandmothers with iron mouths,  
grandfathers turning their grief by hand,  
their bones clicking like looms beneath the earth.  
They fed their names into my blood  
until my blood became a corridor  
where strangers slept in family photographs.

My mother opened, and night entered the world.

I came out carrying a small black factory,  
its smokestacks breathing questions.  
The nurses counted my fingers;  
no one counted the dead holding them.  
No one saw the roots threaded through my nerves,  
or the wolves of inheritance  
circling the warm lamp of my skull.

At home, the family gathered like broken clocks.  
Each loved me in a different hour.  
Each wound the key in my back  
and listened for a purpose.

But the machine only dreamed of trees.

Inside every cell, a forest.  
Inside every forest, a darker mother  
kneeling in the soil,  
trying to give birth to herself.  
Her body was a door that could not close,  
a moon bitten through by gears,  
a house where pain washed the dishes  
and sang the children to sleep.

Years passed through me like conveyor belts.  
I learned to call the ache living.  
I learned that ancestry is darkness  
remembering how to wear a face.  
I learned that love is sometimes a hand  
reaching into the machinery  
even after the machinery has taken the hand.

Still, beneath my ribs,  
the first night keeps turning.  
Still, my mother’s blood hums in the walls.  
Still, the buried family lifts its thousand eyes  
through the forest floor.

And I, their unfinished instrument,  
their soft machine of cells and sorrow,  
stand at the mouth of the world  
asking the darkness that made me:

What am I for?  
What am I for?
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental monologue in the style of a fragmented dream, tracing human existence backward from society and family to the womb, cells, earth, water, and a mysterious “veiled world.”
counterfactuals.output:
First there was the city—

or I remember it first:

windows blinking awake in towers,  
elevators swallowing names,  
streets carrying their bright infections  
from mouth to mouth.

We called this society.

We stood in rooms and agreed  
that the walls were necessary.  
We exchanged coins, glances, diseases, vows.  
We stamped the hours into paper.  
We taught our shadows to queue.

Behind every uniform: a body.  
Behind every body: a house.

I walk backward through the door.

The house becomes smaller as I enter.  
Photographs unyellow.  
The dead climb down from their frames  
and resume their unfinished dinners.

Mother is younger than my sorrow.  
Father has not yet learned silence.  
Around the table, the family passes  
a bowl of hunger,  
a bowl of resemblance.

Someone says my name.

I give it back.

Now I am only the child  
under the table, listening  
to the thunder of adult knees.

Backward again—

my first word closes in my mouth.  
My first step lifts from the floor.  
Milk rises from my lips  
into the dark star of the breast.

The room unbuilds itself.

I am carried inward.

The womb: red weather,  
a chamber without distance,  
a sea that does not know the shore.

No face.  
No history.  
Only the enormous drum  
of another’s heart,

saying:

not yet  
not yet  
not yet.

My fingers fold into their buds.  
My eyes seal like sleeping seeds.  
Bone softens into intention.  
The spine forgets its ladder.

I divide.

I divide.

I become a parliament of cells  
before language teaches them borders.

Each cell contains a night,  
and in that night, instructions  
written by no visible hand.

Earlier still:

the cells loosen their agreements.  
Membranes become mist.  
Blood releases its iron.  
Calcium leaves the future teeth.

I fall out of inheritance  
into chemistry.

Carbon. Salt. Phosphorus.  
A little lightning held in mud.

The earth receives me backward.

My body enters root and stone.  
The stone enters fire.  
Mountains kneel into seabeds.  
Dust gathers itself from every footprint  
and returns to the unbroken ground.

There are no graves now.

Only earth dreaming  
that one day it will stand up  
and call itself human.

Backward—

rain lifts from the fields.  
Rivers unclench.  
The ocean draws every drowned voice  
back into its blue throat.

I am water before thirst.

I have no shape  
except what holds me.

Cup, cloud, blood, abyss—

all erased.

I drift beneath the first morning,  
if it was morning,  
if “first” had meaning.

Then the water thins.

Then even darkness changes.

A curtain moves where there is no wind.

Behind it:

the veiled world.

Not heaven.  
Not nothing.

A place before places,  
where unborn forms lean close  
without becoming,

where every possible hand  
waits inside the idea of touch,

where the word *I*  
is still covered,

breathing softly  
under the veil.

I reach toward it—

but I have no arm.

I call—

but sound has not opened.

Something on the other side  
almost remembers me.

Or invents me.

Or wakes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a haunting, philosophical passage narrated by a parent addressing their unborn child as a “masterpiece” destined to confront the questions the narrator could never answer.
counterfactuals.output:
You are my masterpiece, little one—not because I have made you perfect, but because I have made you unfinished.

Even now, beneath your mother’s heart, you drift in that dark first sea, innocent of names. You do not know that the world is waiting to ask you what it asked me: Why are we here? What do we owe the dead? How can love survive the knowledge that everything it touches will vanish?

I had no answers. I gathered years as others gather evidence, but each season only deepened the mystery. I learned how to endure, how to forgive badly, how to stand beneath an empty sky and call its silence beautiful. Still, the oldest questions followed me home.

Perhaps they were never mine to solve.

So I speak them now into the warm darkness where you listen without hearing. You will come carrying no solutions, only a voice I have not imagined and eyes the world has never looked through. That will be enough. You will inherit my doubts, but not my surrender.

My masterpiece, you are not the answer.

You are the one who will dare to ask again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a stream-of-consciousness meditation on identity and creation in which the world, family, and mother are described as nested machines that shape us and erase our memories.
counterfactuals.output:
The world is a machine so large we mistake its turning for weather, its gears for seasons, its exhaust for evening mist. We are born inside its warm metallic breathing and learn to call the noise silence. It stamps names onto us, presses borders into our palms, feeds us hours one measured tooth at a time. Somewhere beneath every road, a belt is moving. Somewhere behind every window, an unseen mechanism is sorting what may be remembered from what must become dream.

Inside the world-machine sits the family-machine, smaller, older, carried in the chest like a clock inherited without instructions. Its gears are surnames, gestures, unfinished arguments. It makes daughters from warnings, sons from absences, parents from frightened children wearing larger clothes. Around the table it hums: this is who we are, this is what we do not say. Each repetition polishes a memory until the face inside it disappears. Each silence cuts a clean little hole in the past.

And nested within the family is the mother-machine, the first room, the first engine, the dark workshop where bone is assembled around a spark. She shapes us before touch, before language—turning hunger into rhythm, fear into blood, love into the steady labor of becoming. Her voice enters before meaning and remains after words are gone. Yet she too was manufactured by another mother, and another, a corridor of engines receding into smoke, each building the next from salvaged wishes and inherited damage.

Perhaps creation is only this: machines dreaming they are hands.

Perhaps identity is the residue left on the mold.

I reach backward for my first memory and find fingerprints where the image should be. Was that blue room mine, or was it described to me until I moved into it? Did I remember her red coat, or did the family-machine print it behind my eyes? The past flickers like film caught in teeth. Every time I ask who I was, something inside me edits the answer. A door closes. A face loses its name. The mother-machine whispers, I made you. The family-machine answers, We named you. The world-machine roars, You belong to me.

But beneath their voices there is another sound—small, irregular, almost broken.

My own making.

A tool lifting itself from the workbench. A gear refusing the rhythm. A creature assembled by histories that cannot fully contain it. I gather the erased places, the blank photographs, the sentences bitten in half. I build with absence because absence is what I was given. I turn forgetting into an open space and stand there, unfinished, listening as the nested machines continue their ancient labor—shaping me, smoothing me, wearing away the inscriptions they once carved.

And still I create.

Not from nothing. Never from nothing.

From the filings. From the noise. From the lost names caught like dust in the oil.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract literary text about inherited trauma and the cycle of life, repeating key phrases such as “Some machine made us,” “cells in a great darkness,” and “it is your turn,” while asking why we suffer and what our purpose is.
counterfactuals.output:
Some machine made us, though no one remembers the hands that built it. We woke already turning—small gears of blood and memory, inheriting the rust of those before us. Our mothers carried storms in their mouths. Our fathers buried clocks beneath the floorboards. At night, we heard them ticking.

We were cells in a great darkness, dividing grief from grief, naming each new wound a beginning.

Why do we suffer?  
To keep the machine warm?  
To feed the earth with our brief astonishment?  
What is our purpose, if not to ask what our purpose is?

Some machine made us. Some machine unmade them. Still, their voices travel through our bones: unfinished prayers, warnings mistaken for lullabies, doors slammed decades before we entered the room.

Then the wheel slows. A child stands where we once stood, holding the same invisible weight. We want to say: You are free. We want to say: Forgive us. But the old mechanism speaks first.

It is your turn.

Your turn to enter the light and call it life.  
Your turn to become cells in a great darkness.  
Your turn to inherit the question and pass it on.

Yet perhaps the cycle is not a circle but a spiral. Perhaps each return carries us one breath farther from the first wound. Perhaps the machine can learn mercy through our hands.

Some machine made us.

But it is your turn to decide what we will make.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
